clue.text: Artist, modern (by ancient measure) about a second

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the measure wraps around the next piece

parts.note: a cubit is an ancient unit of length, the forearm from elbow to fingertip
S is the standard abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: An art critic describes a painter as modern only by the standards of antiquity, give or take a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cubist belongs to the early twentieth-century school of Picasso and Braque, a modern art movement.

clue.text: Second from last in race failing at the finish

indicators.note: second from last in points to the letter one place before the end of the word race

parts.note: a side that is failing is losing

explanation.surface: A runner in second-to-last place is fading as the line approaches.
explanation.walkthrough: In a four-letter word the second from last letter is the third, C.
explanation.definitionFit: Closing describes what happens at the end, as with closing remarks or the closing stages of a race.

clue.text: Lad gets money and love

parts.note: a buck is slang for a dollar, so money
love is zero in tennis, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A young man comes into some cash and finds romance too.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucko is an informal, chiefly Irish, form of address for a young man or a swaggering fellow.

clue.text: Make-up's second comedy device

parts.note: slap is theatrical slang for stage make-up, and the possessive adds S
a tick is a moment, a second, as in 'back in a tick'

explanation.surface: An actor explains that greasepaint is the second most useful trick in comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapstick is boisterous physical comedy, named after the clapping paddle clowns used to strike each other.

clue.text: Well-pitched motion to claim Yankee heart

indicators.note: heart means the middle, so the Yankee piece is set into the centre of the rearranged word
motion means movement, so the letters of claim are set moving into a new order

parts.note: a Yankee is an American, so US

explanation.surface: A debating motion is proposed to seize the heart of America.
explanation.walkthrough: CLAIM rearranged gives MICAL; 'heart' puts US at its centre, M-US-ICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone musical has a good ear, singing or playing in tune, which is being well-pitched.

clue.text: Bottom note: aah?

parts.note: a minim is a musical note, a half note in American usage
um is a sound of hesitation like aah

explanation.surface: A musician hesitates over the lowest note in the score.
explanation.definitionFit: The minimum is the lowest possible amount, the floor or bottom of a range.

clue.text: Not fresh small beer: what goes into it before being drunk

parts.note: hops are the flavouring plant that goes into beer
oiled is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A drinker muses on stale weak ale and what goes into it before it is swallowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before being' only places the drunk piece after the beer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop-soiled goods are faded or marked from display, so no longer fresh; figuratively worn or stale.

clue.text: Power-sharing puts the French in logical fix

indicators.note: puts ... in means the French article is placed inside the rearranged word
fix suggests the letters of logical are put into a different shape

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: Arranging power-sharing involves bringing French elements into a reasoned arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power-sharing' reads like a political verb phrase but is the adjective defined; 'fix' gives COLGIAL and 'puts ... in' places the article within.
explanation.definitionFit: Collegial describes authority shared equally among colleagues rather than held by one person.

clue.text: Snake's partner — large snake

parts.note: an adder is a venomous snake

explanation.surface: A naturalist notes a big snake keeping company with another.
explanation.walkthrough: In the board game Snakes and Ladders the two always come together.
explanation.definitionFit: In the children's board game snakes are paired with ladders, which carry players up as snakes send them down.

clue.text: Just cradling the head of Lord Nelson's captain

indicators.note: cradling means holding within, so the captain's name surrounds the other letter

parts.note: Thomas Hardy was captain of Nelson's flagship Victory at Trafalgar

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Nelson's captain was merely holding the admiral's head as he died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kiss me, Hardy' were reputedly among Nelson's last words, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardly means only just, barely, as in 'I hardly made it'.

clue.text: Beyond stormy ocean, to win a second time

indicators.note: beyond places the second piece after the first
a stormy sea is churned up, so the letters of ocean are tossed into a new order

parts.note: to win is to gain

explanation.surface: A sailor has crossed a rough ocean and hopes to triumph a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: Once again means repeated, done anew, happening another time.

clue.text: See 5
Endless ridicule at leading store chains

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: irony is mocking language, a form of ridicule

indicators.note: leading means the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Mocking the major retail chains without end.
explanation.definitionFit: Irons are fetters, the shackles and chains used to restrain prisoners.

clue.text: Of dramatic change in play: episode not right

indicators.note: not means the named letter is taken away

parts.note: a drama is a play
a scene is an episode in a play

explanation.surface: A critic notes a sudden twist in a play where one episode goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: DRAMA SCENE loses its R to give DAMA SCENE.
explanation.definitionFit: Damascene refers to a sudden conversion, like Saul's on the road to Damascus, so describes a dramatic change of heart.

clue.text: Good cooking: fry oil and lard with honour

indicators.note: cooking suggests the words fry and oil are worked into a new mixture

explanation.surface: A recipe: frying oil and lard, cooked well, makes a dish fit for honouring.
explanation.definitionFit: To glorify is to praise lavishly, heaping honour on someone; lard here means embellish or cover thickly.

clue.text: Cromwell's "man of iron", a vile distortion

indicators.note: distortion means the letters of the following words are twisted out of shape

explanation.surface: A hostile view of Cromwell's man of iron as a twisted villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link; IRON, A and VILE make the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oliverian was a supporter of Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector nicknamed Old Ironsides.

clue.text: Boatman's second in command put in charge, their leaders half-blind

parts.note: Boatman is the setter, so his own is my

indicators.note: second in picks the second letter of the word command
their leaders means the first letters of the words just before

explanation.surface: The setter's deputy is placed in charge though leaders are half-blind.
explanation.definitionFit: Myopic means short-sighted, seeing only near things clearly, so partly blind.

clue.text: Letters of credit lost, counterfoil torn? Not good conduct

indicators.note: torn means the remaining letters are ripped up and rearranged
lost means the named letters are removed from the word

parts.note: CR is the standard abbreviation for credit

explanation.surface: A bank's paperwork goes missing and the stub is ripped up, which is no way to behave.
explanation.walkthrough: COUNTERFOIL without C and R leaves OUNTEFOIL, which is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaviour that is out of line is improper, crossing accepted bounds of conduct.

clue.text: Finger in food, Indian perhaps

indicators.note: in means the second piece is placed inside the first

parts.note: a pie is a food
Indian ink is one kind of ink, so ink is defined by example

explanation.surface: Someone pokes a finger into food, perhaps a curry.
explanation.definitionFit: The pinkie is the little finger.

clue.text: Second red nose comedy

indicators.note: comedy suggests clowning about, so the letters of red nose are juggled

explanation.surface: Another charity comedy day with red noses.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Nose Day is a British charity telethon of comedy, which the surface evokes.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to support or back it formally.

clue.text: Boatman's senior officer meets destiny

parts.note: a mate is a senior officer on a merchant ship
one's lot is one's destiny or fate

explanation.surface: A setter's ship's officer meets his fate.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelot is British slang, from French, for a sailor, a man of boats.

clue.text: More than a person? Second in command (aye aye, captain!)

indicators.note: second in points to a stretch inside the words, beginning at the second M of command

explanation.surface: A sailor salutes the second in command with a hearty aye aye, captain.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through commAND AYe, starting at the second M; the rest is surface dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-day is a unit of work, one person working one day, so a person plus a day.

clue.text: Sea duty shift on second working day

indicators.note: shift means the letters of sea duty are moved into a new order

explanation.surface: A sailor's sea duty shift falls early in the working week.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuesday follows Monday, so it is the second day of the working week.

clue.text: A summer drink in scenic Eteauville

indicators.note: in means the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A refreshing cold drink enjoyed in a pretty French village in summer.
explanation.walkthrough: Eteauville is an invented village name; the answer runs across scenIC ETEAuville.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea, also called ice tea, is chilled tea served as a summer refreshment.

clue.text: Was Rat to Toad, hence not right?

indicators.note: not right means out of order, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: In The Wind in the Willows, was Ratty ever unfair to Toad?
explanation.walkthrough: Rat and Toad are friends in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows; here rat is a verb, betray.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat on someone is to betray them, so 'was rat to' means betrayed, deceived or was unfaithful.

clue.text: Controversially his (or her) IT crashed

indicators.note: crashed suggests a computer failure, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone's computer, whether a man's or a woman's, has crashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' is a link word; HER and IT give the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Using the plural pronoun for a single person of unknown sex, in place of his, divides grammarians.

clue.text: Second in command to attack with courage

indicators.note: in means the second-place letter goes inside the order

parts.note: fire is the order given to attack with guns
B is second in the alphabet, as in B grade

explanation.surface: A deputy orders an attack, showing bravery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second in command' looks like a deputy, but splits into B inside FIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral fibre is strength of character, so courage or toughness.

clue.text: Allow only formal "thou" in French or Swahili, for example

parts.note: to allow only the formal address is to forbid the familiar one, so ban
tu is the familiar French for you, like English thou

explanation.surface: A language teacher permits only the polite form of address in French.
explanation.walkthrough: Banning tu leaves only formal vous, so 'Allow only formal thou in French' reads as BAN TU.
explanation.definitionFit: Swahili is one of the Bantu family of African languages.

clue.text: Second from last to harvest grain

indicators.note: last to picks the final letter of the word harvest

parts.note: rice is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: A farmer is second to finish bringing in the corn.
explanation.definitionFit: A trice is an instant, a moment, as in 'in a trice'.

clue.text: Changed sides and lied — anger erupted

indicators.note: erupted suggests the letters burst out and land in a new order

explanation.surface: A turncoat lied and there was an outburst of fury.
explanation.definitionFit: To realign is to change allegiance or alignment, so one who realigned switched sides.

clue.text: Second from last in plane perhaps to race here

indicators.note: second from picks the second letter of the word last

parts.note: the plane is a kind of tree, so tree by example

explanation.surface: A flyer second from last on a plane heads off to the races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second from last' looks like a single position, but means the second letter of 'last'. AINTREE is the Liverpool racecourse of the Grand National.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse that hosts the Grand National steeplechase.

clue.text: Record in Nelson's signal his last word to second in command

indicators.note: in means the record is placed within the word

parts.note: Nelson's Trafalgar signal was 'England expects that every man will do his duty', ending in duty
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A recording of Nelson's famous signal ends with a word to his deputy.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy is an assistant who stands in for a superior, the next in rank.
